{{Short description|Result of multiplying seven instances of a number}}
In [[arithmetic]] and [[algebra]], the '''seventh power''' of a [[number]] ''n'' is the result of multiplying seven instances of ''n'' together. So:
:{{math|size=120%|1=''n''<sup>7</sup> = ''n'' × ''n'' × ''n'' × ''n'' × ''n'' × ''n'' × ''n''}}.

Seventh [[power (algebra)|power]]s are also formed by multiplying a number by its [[sixth power]], the [[square number|square]] of a number by its [[fifth power (algebra)|fifth power]], or the [[cube (algebra)|cube]] of a number by its [[fourth power]].

The [[integer sequence|sequence]] of seventh powers of [[integer]]s is:

:0, 1, 128, 2187, 16384, 78125, 279936, 823543, 2097152, 4782969, 10000000, 19487171, 35831808, 62748517, 105413504, 170859375, 268435456, 410338673, 612220032, 893871739, 1280000000, 1801088541, 2494357888, 3404825447, 4586471424, 6103515625, 8031810176, ... {{OEIS|id=A001015}}

In the [[Prime factor exponent notation|archaic notation]] of [[Robert Recorde]], the seventh power of a number was called the "second [[sursolid]]".{{r|womack}}

==Properties==

[[Leonard Eugene Dickson]] studied generalizations of [[Waring's problem]] for seventh powers, showing that every non-negative integer can be represented as a sum of at most 258 non-negative seventh powers{{r|dickson}} (1<sup>7</sup> is 1, and 2<sup>7</sup> is 128). All but finitely many positive integers can be expressed more simply as the sum of at most 46 seventh powers.{{r|kumchev}} If powers of negative integers are allowed, only 12 powers are required.{{r|choudhry}}

The smallest number that can be represented in two different ways as a sum of four positive seventh powers is 2056364173794800.{{r|ekl}} 

The smallest seventh power that can be represented as a sum of eight distinct seventh powers is:{{r|stewart}}
:<math>102^7=12^7+35^7+53^7+58^7+64^7+83^7+85^7+90^7.</math>

The two known examples of a seventh power expressible as the sum of seven seventh powers are

:<math>568^7 = 127^7+ 258^7 + 266^7 + 413^7 + 430^7 + 439^7 + 525^7</math> (M. Dodrill, 1999);{{r|meyrignac}}

and

:<math>626^7 = 625^7+309^7+258^7+255^7+158^7+148^7+91^7</math> (Maurice Blondot, 11/14/2000);{{r|meyrignac}}

Any example with fewer terms in the sum would be a [[counterexample]] to [[Euler's sum of powers conjecture]], which is currently only known to be false for the powers 4 and 5.
